perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent for this trauma profile. As a male firefighter whose index trauma is relief work in a war zone, moral-violation cues are plausible, but 'Babies' and especially 'Comments on sexual violence' imply highly specific trauma-linked content that is not supported anywhere else in the memory, threat, or appraisal items. Those other nodes describe moral injury, disorganized trauma memory, pain recall, anger, and global alienation, but contain no infant-related or sexual-violence-related material. This makes those two triggers feel disconnected from the rest of the formulation rather than part of the same trauma network.

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Feelings' is internally contradictory in wording: 'Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion' describes the opposite of emotional avoidance. It conflicts with the node label and with the rest of the profile, which otherwise suggests suppression/avoidance and control strategies in response to distress. This item is therefore not clinically coherent as selected.

issues.item: Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
issues.explanation: This item directly contradicts the Maladaptive Strategies construct and the rest of the profile. 'Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion' describes openness to emotion rather than avoidance of feelings. It is internally inconsistent within the node, where the other items are clearly maladaptive avoidance/control strategies (self-harm to regulate affect, mental rituals to prevent recurrence), and it does not fit the cognitive formulation linking negative appraisals, memory, and threat to maladaptive coping.

vignette:
Thanh Nguyen is a 46-year-old Vietnamese-American firefighter who presented for psychological evaluation following a period of escalating distress that he described, with visible difficulty, as "things finally getting too loud to ignore." Divorced for three years and living alone in a modest apartment near his fire station, Thanh carries himself with the composed bearing of someone who has spent decades managing other people's emergencies. What brought him to the clinic, however, was something that happened not in a burning building but in a humanitarian deployment he undertook eight years ago, a two-month stint as a relief worker in a conflict zone in Southeast Asia where his firefighting and emergency medical skills were considered assets. It is from those eight weeks that the current clinical picture appears to originate.

Thanh had volunteered with a small international relief organization, and within days of arriving he was working in field conditions for which nothing had prepared him. He witnessed the aftermath of shelling - collapsed structures, fires set deliberately, people pulled from rubble - and was present during an attack on a distribution site in which an explosion occurred close enough to knock him from his feet. The blast threw him hard against a concrete barrier; his left shoulder and the side of his head took the impact. In the chaos that followed, he encountered evidence of systematic sexual violence against women and girls in the camp, including survivors who disclosed what had been done to them while Thanh was among the few personnel present. He was asked to document injuries. He did so, but he has never been able to fully account for the sequence of those hours in his memory. The timeline fractures somewhere around the explosion, and what comes before and after it refuses to arrange itself into a coherent order. He knows things happened - he knows what he saw and what he was asked to do - but when he tries to speak about it, the words dissolve. He has sat across from his former wife, from a station chaplain, from a close colleague, and each time arrived at the same wall: the knowledge present, the language absent.

In the years since returning, Thanh's world has quietly contracted. At the fire station, he functions capably on calls, but the environment carries its own hazards. During a training exercise eighteen months ago, a controlled detonation used to simulate a structural collapse sent him to his knees in the parking lot, heart hammering, certain for several seconds that he was back in the camp. In those moments, a dull, pressured ache rises in his left shoulder and along the left side of his head - the same places that absorbed the impact of the blast - as though the memory carries its own bodily record, insisting on being felt in the precise locations where it first registered. He has since positioned himself during drills so that he is never near the demonstration charges, a small tactical adjustment his colleagues have not questioned. More disruptive is what happens in the station's quieter moments - the long overnight silences between calls. Thanh finds those stretches almost unbearable. He has come to feel that stillness is not rest but warning, that something terrible is accumulating in the quiet, and he has developed a habit of moving through the dormitory, checking on colleagues, manufacturing small sounds, in order to break the silence before it can mean something.

Off duty, he has found himself increasingly reactive in ordinary social situations. When he witnessed a man verbally intimidating a woman at a gas station, he intervened with a force that alarmed him afterward - not because the intervention was wrong, but because the rage that accompanied it felt disproportionate and not entirely his own. Comments overheard about sexual violence, even in news broadcasts or casual conversation, produce a visceral response he struggles to contain. He had come to believe that these reactions confirmed something he feared: that the person who came home from that deployment was not the same person who left, and that the original Thanh - the one who had clear values, a marriage, a sense of where he belonged - had been permanently displaced. What frightened him most was the accompanying conviction that the trauma had not merely changed his life but had demolished it entirely, that the structure of everything he had built - his marriage, his sense of vocation, his place in his own family - was rubble as surely as anything he had pulled people from overseas. He did not feel that he had lost his footing; he felt there was no ground left to stand on. His Vietnamese family gathered on weekends in his parents' home across town, and he had stopped going. His colleagues shared meals and easy conversation in the station kitchen, and he sat outside it. He was certain, in a way that felt less like depression than like clear-eyed assessment, that he no longer belonged anywhere - not to the culture he had grown up in, not to the profession he had chosen, not to the family he had started and then lost. He acted in ways over there, or failed to act in ways, that he cannot reconcile with who he understood himself to be. He does not elaborate on the specifics, but the shame is evident.

To manage the intrusive material, Thanh has developed rituals - specific sequences of thought he runs through before sleep and before certain situations, a private logic he believes may prevent further harm. When the feelings become too large, he has, on several occasions, hurt himself physically, pressing or striking his own body, and he reports this with the matter-of-fact tone of someone describing a pressure valve. The physical pain, he says, is at least a pain he understands. What finally brought him to seek help was his teenage son's recent visit, during which Thanh recognized that he had nothing to offer the boy - no ease, no presence, no sense that his own life had a shape worth inhabiting. He is most afraid, he said at intake, that it is already too late to find out whether it does.

missing.item: Memory: Pain Recall — the vignette does not describe Thanh experiencing physical pain in the same bodily locations as during the traumatic event when the memory returns
missing.explanation: Pain Recall (Memory): Thanh's self-harm is described as deliberately inflicting physical pain to release overwhelming feelings, and the vignette notes physical pain he 'understands.' However, the specific symptom — re-experiencing physical pain in the same body parts as during the traumatic event when the memory returns — is never described. These are clinically distinct phenomena and the latter is absent.

missing.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed — while the vignette conveys loss and contraction, it does not explicitly reflect the belief that his life has been destroyed by the trauma
missing.explanation: Life Destroyed (Negative Appraisals): The vignette conveys that Thanh's world has 'quietly contracted,' his marriage ended, and he feels he has 'nothing to offer.' However, the core belief that the trauma has destroyed his life is not explicitly or clearly paraphrased. The closing reflection gestures toward it but remains ambiguous.

missing.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere — the vignette references loss of his original sense of self and displacement, but does not explicitly capture the feeling that he no longer belongs anywhere
missing.explanation: Belong Nowhere (Negative Appraisals): The vignette states the 'original Thanh' was 'permanently displaced' and that he lost his marriage and sense of self, but the specific appraisal of no longer belonging anywhere — a sense of social/existential rootlessness — is not clearly illustrated or paraphrased in the vignette.
